claim: Under urethane anesthesia, the cortex undergoes spontaneous transitions between states with varying degrees of activation.
source: Under urethane anaesthesia, the cortex undergoes spontaneous transitions between states with varying degrees of 'activation', also known as 'desynchronization' (Clement et al., 2008).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Clement et al., 2008.

claim: During the inactive state, there are globally correlated low-frequency fluctuations in population activity.
source: As shown previously (Curto et al., 2009; Renart et al., 2010), during the inactive state, there are globally correlated low-frequency fluctuations in population activity (Figure 1A; also known as the 'slow oscillation').
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1A showing raster plots.

claim: In the inactive state, there are brief periods when all neurons are silent (down states) separated by periods of firing (up states).
source: In this state, there are brief periods when all neurons are silent (down states) separated by periods of firing (up states).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the up-down state dynamics observed in the data.

claim: During the active state, neurons fire tonically in a globally uncorrelated fashion.
source: In contrast, during the active state, neurons fire tonically in a globally uncorrelated fashion (Figure 1B), as evident from the lack of vertical stripes in the raster (Renart et al., 2010; Ecker et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and citations to previous work.

claim: Rodents rely mainly on ILD to localize sounds in the horizontal plane because they do not use phase information for sound localization.
source: Since rodents do not use phase information for sound localization, they rely mainly on ILD to localize sounds in the horizontal plane (Wesolek et al., 2010; Lauer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wesolek et al., 2010 and Lauer et al., 2011.

claim: Neurons in the auditory cortex in several species, including rats, represent ILD in the form of broad tuning curves with maximum slope at near-zero ILDs.
source: Neurons in the auditory cortex in several species, including rats, represent ILD in the form of broad tuning curves with maximum slope at near-zero ILDs, that is corresponding to sounds arriving from the front of the animal (Stecker et al., 2005; Campbell et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: An increase in overall stimulus intensity (ABL) leads to increased slope of the ILD tuning in inactive sessions.
source: We observed that an increase in overall stimulus intensity (ABL) leads to the increased slope of the ILD tuning: for ABLs 20, 40, and 60 dB, the absolute value of the slope of firing rate regressed on ILD increased from 0.012 to 0.018 to 0.028 (and from 0.022 to 0.026 to 0.048 for onset responses).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific numerical values for the slopes at different ABLs.

claim: In the active state, the responses to different stimuli are similar and strongly overlap without a pronounced monotonic ILD or ABL tuning.
source: In the active state the picture is different (Figure 2D–F). Here, the responses are similar and strongly overlap without a pronounced monotonic ILD or ABL tuning.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figures 2D-F.

claim: In the active state, the tuning curve displays very weak contralateral tuning and is approximately flat near the midline.
source: Especially close to the midline, which is the most critical stimulus region where behavioral accuracy is the highest (Heffner and Heffner, 1988; Recanzone et al., 1998; Recanzone and Beckerman, 2004), the tuning curve displays very weak contralateral tuning and is approximately flat, meaning that all stimuli evoke roughly the same neural response (number of spikes) in the auditory cortex of a single hemisphere.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and cites behavioral studies.

claim: In the active state, the distribution of linear coefficients is roughly symmetric with respect to the horizontal and the vertical axes.
source: In the active state the situation is again different (Figure 3D–F). The distribution of linear coefficients is roughly symmetric with respect to the horizontal and the vertical axes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figures 3D-F.

claim: The tuning heterogeneity in the active state was not explained by the physical location of the neurons in the tissue.
source: This tuning heterogeneity was not explained by the physical location of the neurons in the tissue: it persisted within individual shanks of our recording probes (8 shanks spaced 200 μm apart; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis and references Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Up-down fluctuations in the inactive state induce positive correlations between most neurons.
source: The reason for this is well understood (Renart et al., 2010; Ecker et al., 2014; Okun et al., 2015): up-down fluctuations in the inactive state (Figure 1A) induce positive correlations between most neurons.
evidence: The manuscript explains the mechanism and cites previous work.

claim: In the active state, different stimuli evoke approximately the same number of spikes from the population as a whole.
source: This shows that, in the active state, different stimuli evoke approximately the same number of spikes from the population as a whole, whereas in the inactive state different stimuli evoke different numbers of spikes from the population.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation based on the analysis of the angle between signal plane and global axis.

claim: In the inactive state, the performance of the ILD sign classifier clearly decreases and becomes biased (asymmetric) with decreasing ABL.
source: The performance clearly decreases and becomes biased (asymmetric) with decreasing ABL.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation from the decoding analysis.

claim: In the active state, the neurometric curves for three ABLs strongly overlap, are approximately symmetric, and display little bias.
source: Figure 6B shows the same analysis for the active sessions. Here, the neurometric curves for three ABLs strongly overlap, are approximately symmetric, and display little bias.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 6B.

claim: The JND in the active state ranges from 2.5 to 3.4 dB, which is similar to behavioral values measured in other species.
source: JND ranges from 2.5 to 3.4 which is similar to behavioral values measured in other species (Scott et al., 2007; Keating et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript reports the JND values and cites behavioral studies.

claim: The average JND of rats in a behavioral study was 2.2 dB, slightly smaller than the decoded JND in the active state.
source: We have recently studied ILD discrimination in rats using a subset of stimuli used here with ILDs between ±6 dB (Pardo-Vazquez et al., 2018). The average JND of rats was 2.2 dB, thus just slightly smaller than the decoded JND in the active state.
evidence: The manuscript reports the behavioral JND and cites the study.

claim: The classification accuracy increased with the number of neurons and did not saturate when using all available neurons, either in the active or inactive state.
source: Indeed, we found that the classification accuracy increased with the number of neurons and did not saturate when using all available neurons, either in the active or inactive state (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observation and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the active state, the accuracy increased with the length of the spike count window and did not saturate at 150 ms.
source: We also found that the accuracy increased with the length of the spike count window and did not saturate at 150 ms in the active state.
evidence: The manuscript reports the observation from the time-resolved analysis.

claim: In the inactive state, the decoding accuracy tended to saturate at ~50 ms, converging to an ABL-dependent value.
source: In the inactive state, it did tend to saturate at ~50 ms, converging to an ABL-dependent value (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observation and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the inactive state, the difference in decoding performance between ABLs was pronounced.
source: In recordings of the inactive state, on the other hand, the difference between ABLs was pronounced, in agreement with Figure 6A–B.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figures 6A-B.

claim: In the active state, the sign of ILD can be classified with an ABL-invariant decoder.
source: The difference is absent in the active state, meaning that the sign of ILD can be classified with an ABL-invariant decoder.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation from comparing common and ABL-specialized classifiers.

claim: In the inactive state, the noise correlations impair the accuracy of the code.
source: In other words, the noise correlations in the inactive state impair the accuracy of the code, consistent with our observations above that the noise subspace is aligned with the stimulus subspace in the inactive state.
evidence: The manuscript describes the conclusion from the shuffling analysis.

claim: In the active state, spiking correlations do not significantly constrain the accuracy of the population code.
source: This means that spiking correlations do not significantly constrain the accuracy of the population code during the active state.
evidence: The manuscript describes the conclusion from the shuffling analysis.

claim: Only in the active state the number of significantly tuned neurons increased from the onset (0–50 ms) to the late (100–150 ms) period.
source: Only in the active state the number of significantly tuned neurons increased from the onset (0–50 ms) to the late (100–150 ms) period, which likely explains why decoding accuracy grew monotonically during the evoked response in this state, whereas it saturated after the onset in recordings during inactive states (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observation and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Many neurons in the active state displayed inhibitory responses (below baseline), especially in the late period.
source: Many neurons in the active state displayed inhibitory responses (below baseline, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2), especially in the late period.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The approximate balance of excitatory and inhibitory responses was largely responsible for the weak modulation of the population-averaged response in the active state.
source: The approximate balance of excitatory and inhibitory responses was largely responsible for the weak modulation of the population-averaged response in the active state (Figure 2F) which dropped slightly below baseline in the late period (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the inference and references Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: At the single neuron level, the heterogeneity (and lack thereof) in tuning in the active (inactive) state is maintained in the onset period.
source: At the single neuron level, the heterogeneity (and lack thereof) in tuning in the active (inactive) state is maintained in the onset period (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At the population level, the state dependence of the geometry of the population code is maintained qualitatively if only onset responses are considered.
source: At the population level, the state dependence of the geometry of the population code is also maintained qualitatively if only onset responses are considered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in the prevalence of slow global spiking coordination within cortical circuits can be mediated by changes in the effective level of 'adaptation' present in the circuit.
source: Many studies have suggested that changes in the prevalence of slow global spiking coordination within cortical circuits can be mediated by changes in the effective level of 'adaptation' present in the circuit (Latham et al., 2000; Bazhenov et al., 2002; Compte et al., 2003; Parga and Abbott, 2007; Curto et al., 2009; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2010; Mochol et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this mechanism.

claim: State transitions under urethane resemble those observed between slow-wave and REM sleep, and have the same cholinergic origin.
source: Nevertheless, Clement et al. (2008) found that state transitions under urethane resemble those observed between slow-wave and REM sleep, and have the same cholinergic origin.
evidence: The manuscript cites Clement et al. (2008) for this finding.

claim: Activation of the nucleus basalis, directly or indirectly, desynchronizes the cortex.
source: Activation of the nucleus basalis, directly or indirectly, desynchronizes the cortex (Goard and Dan, 2009; Sakata and Harris, 2012; Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this mechanism.

claim: ACh-induced cortical activation is locally mediated by somatostatin (SOM) interneurons in visual cortex.
source: A recent study found that ACh-induced cortical activation is locally mediated by somatostatin (SOM) interneurons in visual cortex (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Chen et al., 2015 for this finding.

claim: Decision variables in sensory discrimination tasks are posited to involve differences in activity between oppositely tuned populations of neurons.
source: Decision variables in sensory discrimination tasks are posited to involve differences in activity between oppositely tuned populations of neurons (Gold and Shadlen, 2002; Machens et al., 2005; Brunton et al., 2013; Pardo-Vazquez et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this theoretical framework.

claim: Brain activation is seen during behavioral states of attentive wakefulness and active information sampling.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, brain activation is seen during behavioral states of attentive wakefulness and active information sampling (Vanderwolf, 2003; Castro-Alamancos, 2004; Gervasoni et al., 2004; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zagha and McCormick, 2014) during which the brain is presumably actively engaged in identifying the fine structure of the environment.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this observation.

claim: Brain inactivation is observed during immobility or 'automatic' behaviors during wakefulness.
source: Brain inactivation is observed during immobility or 'automatic' behaviors during wakefulness (Vanderwolf, 2003; Castro-Alamancos, 2004; Gervasoni et al., 2004; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zagha and McCormick, 2014), and during slow wave sleep (Steriade et al., 1990; Steriade et al., 1993; Steriade and McCarley, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this observation.

claim: Cortical upstate-onsets coincide with hippocampal sharp-wave-ripples, which are important for memory consolidation.
source: Data showing that cortical upstate-onsets coincide with hippocampal sharp-wave-ripples (Battaglia et al., 2004), which are important for memory consolidation, support this view.
evidence: The manuscript cites Battaglia et al., 2004 for this finding.

claim: States of maximal synchronization and desynchronization both led to errors (misses and false alarms respectively) in auditory detection tasks in mice, with an intermediate state being associated with the best performance.
source: They found that states of maximal synchronization and desynchronization, both led to errors (misses and false alarms respectively), with an intermediate state being associated with the best performance.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings from McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b.

claim: For active states, all sources of variability (ILD, ABL and noise) are reflected in differences in the identity of the responding neurons, and not in the overall number of spikes fired by the population as a whole.
source: We showed that the cortical activation continuum is associated with a complete reorganization of the geometry of the population code that effectively eliminates all influence of the average firing rate during states of strong cortical activation. This means that, for these states, all sources of variability (ILD, ABL and noise) are reflected in differences in the identity of the responding neurons, and not between the overall number of spikes fired by the population as a whole.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: As the cortex becomes more inactive, the identity code becomes progressively replaced by an intensity code.
source: As the cortex becomes more inactive, this identity code becomes progressively replaced by an intensity code, in which the total number of spikes fired by the population reflects both the ILD and ABL of the stimulus and trial-to-trial variability.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: Eighteen adult female Long-Evans rats (240–400 g) were used for electrophysiological recordings.
source: Eighteen adult female Long-Evans rats (240–400 g; Charles River, Italy) were used for electrophysiological recordings in this study.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number and type of animals used.

claim: Seven animals were anesthetized with 1.65 g/kg urethane and the rest with 1.35 g/kg urethane.
source: Seven animals were anesthetized with 1.65 g/kg urethane (solution at 25%, ip) and the rest with 1.35 g/kg urethane (solution at 20%, ip).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the anesthesia protocol.

claim: Extracellular recordings were performed with 64 channel (8 shanks × 8 sites) silicon probes.
source: Extracellular recordings were performed with 64 channel (8 shanks × 8 sites) silicon probes (Buzsaki64, NeuroNexus, Ann Arbor, MI).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the recording equipment used.

claim: Stimuli were 150 ms broadband (5–20 kHz) noise bursts with 5 ms raised-cosine onset/offset ramps.
source: Stimuli were 150 ms broadband (5–20 kHz) noise burst with 5 ms raised-cosine onset/offset ramps generated by a TDT RZ6 module, with 24 bit precision at a 50 kHz sampling rate.
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: A total of 36 combinations (12 ILDs × 3 ABLs) were presented, with each combination presented 100 times.
source: A total of 36 combinations (12 ILDs × 3 ABLs) were presented. ILDs were ±1.5, ±3, ±4.5, ±6, ±12, and ±20 dB; ABLs were 20, 40 and 60 dB SPL. Negative ILD values correspond to stimuli with higher intensity to the left ear (contralateral to the recording hemisphere). Each combination was presented 100 times, in pseudorandom order, with all 36 combinations being presented every 36 trials (except for rat #1 where stimuli were chosen randomly; this rat had 67–138 repetitions per stimulus, with the same 3600 overall).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the stimulus presentation protocol.

claim: The inter-stimulus interval changed randomly between 850 and 1150 ms across presentations.
source: The inter-stimulus interval changed randomly between 850 and 1150 ms across presentations.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the inter-stimulus interval.
